title: How Urvi works today (V 1.0 demo)
intro: Single-Agent, Multi-Tool Hybrid Architecture — natural spoken & typed language in (Gemini ADK / Live) → deterministic engineering physics, ML models & numeric-grounding guards underneath (best of both worlds with minimal hallucination). Urvi is one AI agent with a set of engineering tools. The AI model understands the question and decides which tools to call; the tools do the calculations on well data; the model then explains the result in a few sentences. The model never invents numbers.

sections.heading: Three ways a request is handled

rows: A plain screen command, e.g. "full screen", "Mangala dikhao", "show me the architecture"
A rule-based parser in the browser changes the screen directly
A typed question, e.g. "Which field is underperforming?"
The ADK agent: one agent on Gemini 3.8 Flash with 34 tools
Gemini 3.8 Live through our Live proxy, with 13 voice tools (ADK is not used for voice)

sections.heading: A typed question, step by step
steps: You type in the Urvi panel. The browser checks whether it is a plain screen command; if not, it sends the question to the Urvi API, with the screen context (field, well, language).
A Python web service (FastAPI) on Cloud Run (urvi-cairn-app) receives the request at /api/chat. It also serves the web app itself.

The API hands the question to the agent, built with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK). There is one agent, named "urvi_agent". Its instructions describe the 5-level drill-down (field → health → priority list → well → next best action) and which tool answers what.

The agent sends the question and the tool list to Gemini. Gemini replies with the tool(s) to call, e.g. compare_fields. After the tools run, it gets their results back and writes a short answer (2–4 sentences).
Each tool is ordinary Python code: decline attribution, well health, ranking, next best action, document search, and so on. Several tools can be called in one turn.
The tools read the well tables (production, pressures, completion, job history) through the data access layer. In the demo these are synthetic parquet files packed into the app.

The answer goes back to the browser together with screen actions, so the matching view opens (chart, completion diagram, recommendation). A guard checks that every number in the answer appears in a tool result; any other number is masked.

sections.heading: A spoken question, step by step
steps: The browser streams your microphone (16 kHz) over a WebSocket to the Gemini Live proxy on our server, and plays Urvi's spoken reply (24 kHz). You can interrupt at any time. If the connection drops (network blip, laptop sleep), the browser reconnects by itself and, if it ever falls back to text, retries voice every 20 seconds.

The proxy connects to Gemini Live, a speech-to-speech model. It hears the question, decides which voice tool to call, and speaks the answer in one fixed voice (Aoede). Indian English by default; switch to any of 15 Indian languages (Punjabi, Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu and more) by asking or from the language menu, and the speech locale follows. Short drops are resumed on the server (6 tries) before it falls back to text.

Voice tools run on our server and call the same analytics code as chat. There are fewer of them (13) because a voice model works best with a short list; some bundle several chat tools, e.g. well_profile also returns offset decline, anomalies and wax / sand. The slowest calculations are warmed when the server starts, so the first answer comes in about a second.

sections.heading: Is it a multi-agent system?
body: No. Urvi is a single agent with many tools: one ADK agent for chat and one Gemini Live session for voice. There are no sub-agents and no agent-to-agent hand-offs.
The design allowed splitting into specialist sub-agents if the agent picked the wrong tool too often (below 90%). The evaluation scored 46 of 46 (100%), so one agent is enough.
How to say it: "One Urvi agent with 34 engineering tools for chat, and the same tools through Gemini Live for voice. Every number comes from deterministic tools, never from the model."

sections.heading: Where the recommendations come from
body: The next-best-action tool combines physics checks (water/polymer breakthrough diagnostics, pump signatures, offset wells, pressure surveys), a trained intervention classifier, historical success rates and look-alike wells, and returns a ranked top 3 with probability of success, expected gain, rig-days and the SOP.
Full explanation, with a worked example: docs/ml_recommendation_engine.md.

sections.heading: Data, build and identity (the grey lines)
body: Data: a seeded generator creates 460 synthetic wells across Barmer Basin (Mangala, Bhagyam, Aishwariya, Raageshwari; 60 months). The app reads parquet copies packed into the container; the same data sits in gs://urvi-cairn-barmer-ai-agent-datalake and a BigQuery medallion lakehouse (urvi_cairn_bronze → urvi_cairn_silver → urvi_cairn_gold) in Mumbai (asia-south1).
Build: Cloud Build builds the container image and stores it in Artifact Registry; Cloud Run runs urvi-cairn-app as one instance (sessions are kept in memory).
Identity: Cloud Run runs as a dedicated service account and reaches Gemini and BigQuery without API keys.

sections.heading: Why the demo runs in the US region
body: Gemini Live is not yet offered in India regions, so the demo runs in us-central1. It uses only synthetic data. The production design runs in India regions: see the Target view.
